reconstruction: This exact formal characterization is our consequence of the preceding isomorphism. We do not replace the informal request for a range description by an unrecorded continuation problem.
fate: The character transform is already developed in \citet[\S3]{amice1965mesures}; the exponential-coordinate formulation here follows by a change of formal variable. No distinct publication or unresolved analytic-domain question is identifiable from the notebook wording.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: The bounded formal range is determined by the transform theorem. A broader analytic range question lacks a specified domain and topology.

title: The Newton--Mahler expansion and norm identity
notes: The proof uses \(P_k(x)=x(x-1)\cdots(x-k+1)/k!\), \(c_k=\Delta^kf(0)\), and claims uniform convergence for every continuous \(f\), with \(\max|f|=\max|a_k|\). The series is called Taylor and then Maclaurin.
statement: Every \(f\in C(\mathbb Z_p,K)\) has the unique uniformly convergent expansion \(f(x)=\sum_{k\ge0}c_k\binom{x}{k}\), where \(c_k=\sum_{j=0}^k(-1)^{k-j}\binom{k}{j}f(j)\to0\), and \(\|f\|_\infty=\sup_k|c_k|\). Duality gives \(\|\mu\|=\sup_k|\int\binom{x}{k}\,d\mu|\). These are finite differences and falling factorials, not derivatives and ordinary powers.
reconstruction: The vanishing of the coefficients and uniqueness are supplied. The \(a_k\) in the last norm formula refers to function-expansion coefficients there; elsewhere it denotes measure moments.
fate: This is Mahler's 1958 interpolation theorem \citep[Theorem~1]{mahler1958interpolation}, extended in \citet[Chapter~II]{amice1964interpolation}. Mahler's 1961 correction concerns the differentiability theorem, not this continuous expansion \citep[opening paragraph]{mahler1961correction}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established; the notebook name ``Maclaurin must not be read as a claim of ordinary analyticity for every continuous p-adic function.

title: Quillen's Q-category of an exact category
notes: \(M\) is an additive full subcategory of an abelian category, closed under extensions. Objects of \(QM\) are those of \(M\); a morphism is drawn \(X\leftarrow X''\to X'\), with an admissible epimorphism and an admissible monomorphism.
statement: Let \(\mathcal M\) be an essentially small extension-closed additive full subcategory of an abelian category, with the induced exact structure. A morphism \(X\to Y\) in \(Q\mathcal M\) is an isomorphism class of spans \(X\xleftarrow{p}Z\xrightarrow{i}Y\), with \(p\) an admissible epimorphism and \(i\) an admissible monomorphism. Composition uses pullback; the exact-category axioms ensure admissibility.
reconstruction: We insert smallness, the induced exact structure, equivalence of spans, and the composition law. These are necessary to turn the diagram into a category.
fate: \citet[\S2, construction of \(Q\mathcal M\)]{quillen1973higher} is the exact source, originating in the 1972 Seattle lectures and published in 1973. This continues the exposition in record 311.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established; there is no separate Fuchs conjecture here.

title: The missing loop in comparison with the plus construction
notes: The notebook states that \(BQM\) is homologically equivalent to \(B\operatorname{GL}(\infty,A)\).
statement: For a unital ring \(A\), let \(\mathcal P(A)\) be its exact category of finitely generated projective modules. Then \(\Omega BQ\mathcal P(A)\simeq K_0(A)\times B\operatorname{GL}(A)^+\), after choosing compatible base components. Thus the component of the constant loop has the homotopy type of \(B\operatorname{GL}(A)^+\), and the plus map from \(B\operatorname{GL}(A)\) is an integral homology equivalence. The statement does not concern \(BQ\mathcal P(A)\) itself.
reconstruction: The ring, category, loop-space shift, and component are supplied. For example \(H_1(BQ\mathcal P(\mathbb F_2))\cong K_0(\mathbb F_2)=\mathbb Z\), whereas \(H_1(B\operatorname{GL}(\mathbb F_2))=0\), so the literal line cannot be retained.
fate: The comparison is announced in \citet[introduction, pp.~86--87]{quillen1973higher}, which expressly defers its proof; see the later treatment in \citet[Chapter~IV, Q-construction]{weibel2013kbook}. The corrected theorem was already available in the 1972--1973 work.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established with the loop and component restored. The displayed notebook comparison is false as written.

title: K-zero as the fundamental group of BQ
notes: The Grothendieck group is generated by objects with relations \(X=X'+X''\) from short exact sequences; the notes identify it with \(K_0(M)=\pi_1(BQM,0)\).
statement: For an essentially small exact category \(\mathcal M\), let \(K_0(\mathcal M)\) be the abelian group on isomorphism classes \([X]\), modulo \([X]=[X']+[X'']\) for every admissible short exact sequence. There is a canonical isomorphism \(K_0(\mathcal M)\cong\pi_1(BQ\mathcal M,0)\).
reconstruction: Isomorphism classes and admissibility are explicit. The split exact sequences explain commutativity but do not replace the nonsplit relations.
fate: This is the basic \(K_0\)-identification in \citet[\S2]{quillen1973higher}, circulated in the 1972 Seattle lectures and published in 1973.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: A standard theorem; the indexing of homotopy groups is correct in this line.

title: Object loops and additivity through two-simplices
notes: For each \(X\), the sketch defines a loop \(\zeta_X\) through \(0\) and \(X\). The triangular picture for \(0\to X'\to X\to X''\to0\) yields \(\zeta_X\sim\zeta_{X'}\zeta_{X''}\), invoking two-simplices.
statement: There are two canonical \(Q\)-arrows \(0\to X\): the spans \(0\leftarrow0\to X\) and \(0\leftarrow X\xrightarrow{1}X\). Traversing the first and then the reverse of the second gives a based loop, with a choice of global sign convention. The nerve's two-simplices associated with an admissible exact sequence identify its class with the product of the corresponding classes for \(X'\) and \(X''\).
reconstruction: The backwards path is a path in the realization, not an inverse morphism in \(Q\mathcal M\). We spell out the spans to disambiguate the diagram.
fate: This is the elementary nerve proof underlying \citet[\S2, calculation of \(\pi_1\)]{quillen1973higher}, not a new additivity theorem.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: An identifiable proof of the preceding theorem; the diagram is meaningful after distinguishing arrows from reversed paths.

title: Darboux coordinates and symplectic transition functions
notes: Locally \(\omega=\sum dp_k\wedge dq_k\), and tangent-bundle transition maps lie in \(\operatorname{Sp}(2n,\mathbb R)\). They are assumed lifted to the two-sheeted cover.
statement: Every smooth symplectic \(2n\)-manifold has Darboux charts in which \(\omega\) has the displayed form. Derivatives of coordinate changes preserve \(\omega\) and therefore are symplectic linear maps pointwise. A metaplectic structure is a compatible cocycle of lifts, not merely separate lifts of individual transition functions.
reconstruction: We distinguish nonlinear coordinate changes from their derivatives, and impose the cocycle condition on the lifts.
fate: This is the local and bundle background used in \citet[\S3]{krysl2017spinors}; the topological obstruction is item 1973-312.1. No new local normal-form theorem is proposed.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Standard Darboux and principal-bundle theory.

title: The Schwartz--Hilbert--distribution triple of spinor bundles
notes: The spinor representation induces \(HM\), with \(SM\subset HM\subset S'M\); \(SM\) is labelled rapidly decreasing.
statement: Given a metaplectic principal bundle \(P\to M\), the invariant triple \(\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)\subset L^2(\mathbb R^n)\subset\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)\) yields associated bundles \(P\times_{\operatorname{Mp}}\mathcal S\), \(P\times_{\operatorname{Mp}}L^2\), and \(P\times_{\operatorname{Mp}}\mathcal S'\). The Hilbert embedding in tempered distributions uses the usual pairing convention. These are infinite-dimensional bundles with their respective locally convex topologies.
reconstruction: The fibre models, topology, and chosen metaplectic structure are supplied; \(S'M\) is a distribution bundle, not the algebraic dual of all sections.
fate: The spinor bundle and oscillator realization are described in \citet[\S\S2.2--3.1]{krysl2017spinors}; \citet[\S3, Definition~2]{krysl2006spinor} also constructs the associated bundle. This records Kostant's existing construction.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: An established construction. The representation preserves Schwartz space, so the three fibres glue compatibly.

title: The Heisenberg bundle and the polynomial degree error
notes: \(GM=TM\oplus(\mathbb R\times M)\) is called the Heisenberg Lie algebra bundle and is labelled polynomials of degree at most two in \(p,q\). It acts on the spinor bundle.
statement: The fibre \(T_xM\oplus\mathbb R\) with \([(v,a),(w,b)]=(0,\omega_x(v,w))\) is the \((2n+1)\)-dimensional Heisenberg Lie algebra. Under Poisson brackets it corresponds to affine-linear polynomials, of degree at most one. Polynomials of degree at most two form the larger semidirect extension by \(\mathfrak{sp}(2n,\mathbb R)\). Its infinitesimal Schrödinger action is defined on the Schwartz fibres, not as bounded operators on every Hilbert fibre.
reconstruction: We repair the degree and specify the invariant domain of the action. The central normalization may be rescaled consistently.
fate: The Heisenberg and Weyl-algebra realization is standard background in \citet[\S\S2.1--2.3]{krysl2017spinors}. A dimension count already separates the two polynomial algebras.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: The named Heisenberg construction is established; the degree-two label is a faithful notebook error.

title: Lagrangian tangent planes
notes: The final line introduces \(RM\) and \(R_x\), Lagrangian subspaces of \(T_xM\) of maximal dimension.
statement: A subspace \(L\subset T_xM\) is Lagrangian if \(\omega_x|_L=0\) and \(\dim L=n\), equivalently \(L=L^{\perp_\omega}\). All such planes form the fibre of the Lagrangian Grassmannian bundle over \(M\). A global section is additional structure and is not asserted to exist.
reconstruction: The equality of maximal isotropic dimension with half the tangent dimension is made explicit. The notation does not identify a chosen polarization.
fate: This is standard symplectic linear algebra in the setting reviewed by \citet[\S3]{krysl2017spinors}; Fuchs's short intervention on P000529 continues the bundle description.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: An established definition, with no existence theorem for a Lagrangian distribution in the notes.

title: The nonlinear chain equation and its Hamiltonian sign
notes: The displayed chain has \(\ddot x_k=x_{k-1}+x_{k+1}-2x_k+\varepsilon(x_{k-1}-x_k)^2+\varepsilon(x_{k+1}-x_k)^2\). Both nonlinear signs are positive in the scan.
statement: For a nearest-neighbour Hamiltonian chain with \(r_k=x_{k+1}-x_k\), potential \(V(r)=r^2/2+\varepsilon r^3/3\), and compatible fixed or periodic boundary conditions, \(\ddot x_k=V'(r_k)-V'(r_{k-1})\). Hence the quadratic terms occur as \(\varepsilon[(x_{k+1}-x_k)^2-(x_k-x_{k-1})^2]\). The notebook equation is a different dynamical system unless an omitted convention changes the model.
reconstruction: The Hamiltonian and boundary-condition alternatives specify the standard alpha-FPU reconstruction. We do not silently edit the source or claim that its plus-plus equation has the same conservation law.
fate: The FPU numerical experiment was reported in \citet[LA-1940]{fermipastaulam1955studies}, written in May 1955. The primary report record was checked; the Hamiltonian differentiation above supplies the sign check independently.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: The standard FPU model is identifiable, but its equation is not faithfully represented by the two nonlinear plus signs.

title: Numerical recurrence of low-mode energy
notes: For a chain labelled 16, the initial displacement is sinusoidal, with all energy in the first harmonic. The sketch shows transfer to other modes and near return. A cubic nonlinearity is said to give the same qualitative result.
statement: The identifiable claim is an observation for particular finite nonlinear chains and initial conditions: modal energies may show pronounced near recurrence rather than rapid equipartition. It is not exact periodicity, not a statement for every initial condition, and not a bound uniform in chain length or energy.
reconstruction: We distinguish a numerical observation from a quantified theorem. The notebook does not specify amplitudes, coupling strength, endpoint convention, or the formula used to define modal energy.
fate: The phenomenon is the already reported FPU experiment \citep[LA-1940]{fermipastaulam1955studies}; the connection with soliton recurrence was studied by \citet[pp.~240--243]{zabuskykruskal1965solitons}. Both precede the talk.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: The historical phenomenon is established, but the particular plotted experiment is not reproducible from these notes alone.

title: Unidentified recurrence times and integration-step comments
notes: The notes contain \(t=10^{-35}\), a caption approximately 50 million periods, and comments about ten steps and a one-third period. No physical units or numerical algorithm are given.
statement: No definite numerical estimate can be reconstructed: it is not stated which time scale, error tolerance, integration scheme, or physical system the numbers refer to. The figure supports only the qualitative recurrence item 1973-316.2.
reconstruction: We retain the negative exponent seen in the scan rather than changing it to match a plausible timescale. The disconnected numbers are not used as data for a computation.
fate: Comparison with the identifiable FPU report \citep[LA-1940]{fermipastaulam1955studies} does not determine these units or the stated step counts. No exact numerical publication match was found.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Unidentified numerical details, not an open recurrence-time conjecture.

title: Zakharov's integrable approximation explanation
notes: Zakharov proposes approximation by a differential system possessing first integrals as a possible cause of recurrence. A sinusoidally excited string is mentioned, followed by the remark that other initial data can lead to equipartition.
statement: In a long-wavelength, weak-nonlinearity scaling, an FPU chain may be approximated over a specified time regime by a dispersive PDE such as KdV. Integrability can explain recurrent or coherent behaviour in that regime; it does not imply exact integrability of the original chain or exclude later energy transfer. The recorded equipartition remark has no universal quantifiers or rate.
reconstruction: The scaling restrictions and limitation of the approximation are supplied. The notes propose an explanation, not a convergence theorem with an error bound.
fate: The KdV and recurrence connection was already explored by \citet[pp.~240--243]{zabuskykruskal1965solitons} in 1965. The notebook's attribution to Zakharov concerns this seminar intervention, not priority for the general connection.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: A recognizable established mechanism, with no precise new approximation or equipartition problem in the notes.
speaker: V. E. Zakharov

title: Periodic trajectories of the wave equation on a circle
notes: For \(u_{tt}=u_{xx}\) on \(S^1\), the notes say all trajectories are closed.
statement: On a circle of length \(2\pi\), an energy solution has Fourier modes \(a_n\cos(nt)+b_n\sin(nt)\) for \(n\ne0\) and constant mode \(a_0+b_0t\). The solution is \(2\pi\)-periodic in the energy phase space if and only if the mean initial velocity \(b_0\) is zero. The spatially constant solution \(u(t,x)=t\) refutes the unrestricted assertion.
reconstruction: The circle length and phase space are fixed for precision. The missing zero-mode hypothesis is diagnosed directly by Fourier series, not inferred as something the speaker necessarily said.
fate: Elementary Fourier analysis gives both the corrected theorem and the explicit counterexample. This is old background within the discussion, not a later resolution of a research problem.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Correct on the zero-mean-velocity subspace; false for the full phase space.

title: Periodic first-order drift for a cubic perturbation
notes: The equations \(u_{tt}=u_{xx}+\varepsilon f'(u)\) and \(u_{tt}=u_{xx}-\varepsilon u^3\) are followed by the claim that the first-order drift of trajectories is also periodic.
statement: The recorded statement lacks the averaged vector field, its domain, treatment of the zero mode, and the meaning of periodicity. Consequently neither a universal periodicity theorem for an averaged flow nor periodicity of every solution of the nonlinear PDE is a supported precise formulation.
reconstruction: We preserve the claim without supplying an unrecorded normal-form or averaging construction. The nonlinear equation alone does not determine which drift system is intended.
fate: Searches combining Schnirelman/Shnirelman, periodic wave equations, first-order averaging, and FPU recurrence did not identify an exact theorem with these quantifiers. The familiar integrable-approximation literature is only thematic and cannot fill the gap.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Not identifiable as a definite theorem or open problem from the available notes.

title: The bundle of Lagrangian planes
notes: The box headed Fuchs defines \(\Lambda\) as the set of Lagrangian planes in \(\mathbb R^{2n}\) and depicts \(RM\to M\), a bundle of Lagrangian planes on a symplectic manifold.
statement: For the symplectic frame bundle \(\operatorname{Fr}_{\operatorname{Sp}}(TM)\), form \[\Lambda(TM)=\operatorname{Fr}_{\operatorname{Sp}}(TM)\times_{\operatorname{Sp}(2n,\mathbb R)}\Lambda(n)\longrightarrow M,\qquad \Lambda(n)\cong U(n)/O(n).\] Its fibre consists of all Lagrangian subspaces of \(T_xM\). A section is a Lagrangian distribution, which need not be integrable or globally exist.
reconstruction: The associated-bundle formula and homogeneous-space description explicate the picture. No Maslov class or global section is attributed to the notebook.
fate: This is standard symplectic bundle geometry in the framework reviewed by \citet[\S3]{krysl2017spinors}; the brief source gives only the construction, not a distinct research claim.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established background, continuing item 1973-315.4.

title: Nonsingular Hermitian forms over a ring with involution
notes: A matrix \(\lambda\) over \(\Lambda\) is called a quadratic form when \(\lambda^*=\lambda\) and \(\mu\lambda=1\) for some \(\mu\).
statement: Let \(\Lambda\) be a unital ring with involution and \(\lambda\in M_n(\Lambda)\) satisfy \(\lambda^*=\lambda\) and \(\mu\lambda=1\). Taking adjoints gives \(\lambda\mu^*=1\); uniqueness of a left and right inverse yields \(\mu=\mu^*\), so \(\lambda\) is invertible. It defines a nonsingular Hermitian form on the free module. Over rings where two is not invertible, this is not the same data as a quadratic refinement in surgery theory.
reconstruction: The term Hermitian is used for the actual displayed matrix conditions. The source's one-sided inverse is sufficient because self-adjointness provides the other side.
fate: Hermitian forms are older background. The self-adjoint invertible matrix setting over a group ring is explicit in \citet[\S3]{mishchenko1973infinite}, published before the seminar; the general ring exposition is \citet[\S3]{mishchenko1974signatures}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established; the matrix definition is precise after distinguishing Hermitian forms from quadratic refinements.

title: Fredholm representations
notes: \(T=(T_1,F,T_2)\), where the \(T_i\) are involution-preserving representations and \(F\) is Fredholm with \(FT_1(x)-T_2(x)F\) compact for every \(x\in\Lambda\).
statement: Take unital star representations \(T_i:\Lambda\to\mathcal B(H_i)\) and a bounded Fredholm operator \(F:H_1\to H_2\) satisfying the stated compact-intertwining condition. For \(\Lambda=\mathbb Z[\pi]\), unitary representations of \(\pi\) extend to this data. Different Hilbert spaces are allowed.
reconstruction: The two Hilbert spaces, boundedness, and unit-preserving condition are explicit. Compactness is pointwise for each ring element; no unrecorded uniform bound on the whole ring is imposed.
fate: The group version already appears in \citet[\S1]{mishchenko1973infinite}, received 10 October 1972 and published in the March--April 1973 issue. The general ring definition is \citet[Definition~1.1]{mishchenko1974signatures}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: An established precursor of Fredholm-module formulations of K-homology.

title: Spectral splitting and the compact off-diagonal blocks
notes: The represented forms are bounded, self-adjoint and invertible. In positive/negative decompositions, \(F\otimes1\) has compact off-diagonal entries and Fredholm diagonal entries. The lower right entry is first written \(F_3\), then called \(F_4\).
statement: Let \(\lambda_i=T_i^{(n)}(\lambda)\), and split \(H_i^n=H_i^+\oplus H_i^-\) by their spectral projections. The relation \(F^{(n)}\lambda_1-\lambda_2F^{(n)}\in\mathcal K\) implies that the two off-diagonal blocks of \(F^{(n)}\) are compact. Since \(F^{(n)}\) is Fredholm, its diagonal blocks \(F_+:H_1^+\to H_2^+\) and \(F_-:H_1^-\to H_2^-\) are Fredholm.
reconstruction: The decomposition is spectral, not a finite-dimensional diagonalization by an eigenbasis. Functional calculus modulo compact operators justifies preservation of spectral signs because zero is separated from the spectra.
fate: The splitting lemma was stated in \citet[\S3]{mishchenko1973infinite}; \citet[Lemmas~3.2--3.3]{mishchenko1974signatures} gives the fuller proof. The notebook has an index typo.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established for the bounded invertible represented forms; the corrected lower right block is the negative-to-negative block.

title: The T-signature of a form
notes: \(\operatorname{sign}_T\lambda=\operatorname{index}F_1-\operatorname{index}F_4\), independent of the splitting and of the representative of the form class.
statement: With the spectral blocks of item 1973-318.3, define \(\operatorname{Sign}_T(\lambda)=\operatorname{ind}F_+-\operatorname{ind}F_-\). It is invariant under isometry of nonsingular forms, additive under orthogonal sum, and zero on hyperbolic forms, hence descends to the corresponding Witt/L-group under the conventions of the construction.
reconstruction: We identify precisely the equivalences required for descent. This is not a claim of invariance under an unspecified relation on arbitrary singular matrices.
fate: The index difference and its well-defined Wall-group homomorphism are explicit in \citet[\S3]{mishchenko1973infinite}. The fuller account is \citet[Definition~3.4 and Theorem~3.5]{mishchenko1974signatures}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established; the index difference, not the sum, is the signature invariant.

title: The Fredholm-representation higher-signature formula
notes: For compact \(M\) of dimension \(4K\), \(\pi_1(M)=\pi\), and \(\Lambda=\mathbb Z[\pi]\), the notes state \(\operatorname{sign}_T\sigma(M)=\langle\operatorname{ch}\xi_T\,L(M),[M]\rangle\). They call \(\xi_T\) a bundle and \(\sigma(M)\) a quadratic form.
statement: Let \(M\) be a closed oriented smooth \(4k\)-manifold, \(f:M\to B\pi\) the classifying map of its universal cover, and \(T\) a Fredholm representation of \(\pi\). With Mishchenko's Wall/Poincare-complex class \(\sigma(M)\) and associated K-theory class \(\xi_T\) pulled back along \(f\), \[\operatorname{Sign}_T\sigma(M)=\langle L(TM)\smile\operatorname{ch}(f^*\xi_T),[M]\rangle.\] The coefficient class is virtual in general; constructing \(\sigma(M)\) uses the algebraic Poincare complex, not an unjustified free middle-homology module.
reconstruction: Closedness and orientation, the classifying map, the virtual K-class, and the surgery-theoretic meaning of \(\sigma(M)\) are supplied.
fate: The exact formula is \citet[Theorem~1]{mishchenko1973infinite}, publicly printed before this talk. \citet[Theorem~5.1]{mishchenko1974signatures} gives the full treatment; announcement and full result were read.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: The formula is established for the classes produced by Fredholm representations. It is not a proof of the Novikov conjecture for every group and every cohomology class.

title: Why finite-dimensional representations do not suffice
notes: The talk ends ``\ru{Конечномерных предст. недостаточно}''; the ordinary Hirzebruch signature is indicated by \(\operatorname{ch}\xi_T=1\).
statement: A complex vector bundle associated to a finite-dimensional unitary representation of \(\pi\) is flat. Its positive-degree rational Chern character vanishes, so the corresponding characteristic number sees only its rank times the ordinary signature. Fredholm representation pairs can produce nontrivial K-classes with higher-degree Chern character. This explains the need for the infinite-dimensional construction, without asserting that all K-classes arise this way for every group.
reconstruction: The rational qualification and the limitation on representability of arbitrary K-classes are essential to the interpretation.
fate: Flat-bundle rational Chern classes are older background. The pre-talk \citet[Theorem~3 and corollary]{mishchenko1973infinite} exhibits the reach of infinite-dimensional families under geometric assumptions; \citet[introduction and \S6]{mishchenko1974signatures} explains the motivation. These stronger geometric conclusions are not imported into the notebook.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: An established motivation, not a universal representability theorem.

title: Lattice operations, order and distributivity
notes: Two associative, commutative, idempotent operations \(\cap,+\) satisfy absorption. The order is \(a\le b\iff a\cap b=a\). Distributive lattices are described as systems of subsets.
statement: A lattice has meet \(a\wedge b\) and join \(a\vee b\) satisfying those identities; they determine the stated partial order. Distributivity is either, equivalently both, distributive identities. Every distributive lattice embeds into a lattice of subsets with intersection and union (with the usual prime-ideal separation principle); it need not be the entire powerset, nor be closed under complements.
reconstruction: We interpret ``systems of subsets'' as a sublattice representation, not a Boolean-algebra assertion. The conventional separation principle is explicit.
fate: These are the introductory definitions, also reproduced in \citet[\S1.1]{gelfandponomarev1974modular}; they were standard before 1973.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established elementary lattice theory.

title: The modular law for submodule lattices
notes: For \(a\subseteq b\), \(b\cap(a+c)=a+(b\cap c)\), called Dedekind's law. Subspace and submodule lattices are modular but not generally distributive.
statement: For submodules \(A\subseteq B\) and \(C\) of a module over any unital ring, \(B\cap(A+C)=A+(B\cap C)\). Thus its submodule lattice is modular. A vector space of dimension at least two has a nondistributive subspace lattice: three distinct lines in a two-dimensional subspace violate distributivity. Dimensions zero and one are exceptions to the notebook's unqualified phrase.
reconstruction: The dimension restriction is supplied; modularity needs no finite-dimensionality assumption.
fate: This is standard background, stated in \citet[\S1.1]{gelfandponomarev1974modular}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established, with the low-dimensional distributive cases separated.

title: Are all modular lattices submodule lattices?
notes: The notes ask whether there are further identities and explicitly conjecture that every modular lattice is the lattice of submodules of a module; they immediately note that subspace lattices have further identities.
statement: The literal conjecture is false. Submodule lattices satisfy the Arguesian (lattice-theoretic Desargues) identity, whereas a non-Desarguesian projective plane gives a modular lattice of height three that fails it. Such a lattice is neither isomorphic to a full submodule lattice nor embeddable as a sublattice of one. Modularity alone is therefore insufficient.
reconstruction: The exact conjecture concerns submodules, not merely vector subspaces. We use the older Arguesian obstruction to answer that literal formulation; we do not replace it by an unspecified coordinatization problem.
fate: The relevant extra condition was studied in \citet[pp.~294--313]{jonsson1954modular}, published in 1954. The submodule necessity is also stated explicitly in \citet[\S6]{herrmanntakach2005subgroup}. The conjecture was thus already false in the established theory, despite its appearance as a question in the notebook.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Disproved; the non-Desarguesian-plane obstruction answers the recorded universal assertion.

title: Free modular lattices and linear equivalence of terms
notes: \(D^r\) is generated by \(e_1,\ldots,e_r\) modulo modular-lattice relations. Terms \(P,Q\) are linearly equivalent if they agree after substituting subspaces.
statement: The free modular lattice \(D^r\) has the universal property for assignments of its generators to any modular lattice. For this notebook's finite-dimensional representation setting, define \(a\sim b\) if \(\rho(a)=\rho(b)\) for every lattice homomorphism \(\rho:D^r\to\mathcal L(V)\), every field \(k\), and every finite-dimensional \(k\)-space \(V\). This congruence can identify distinct abstract lattice elements.
reconstruction: The quantifiers over fields and finite dimensions follow the subsequent definition of perfect elements. Abstract equality and equality in every linear representation remain separate.
fate: \citet[\S1.2]{gelfandponomarev1974modular} gives precisely this notion and notes that distinct linearly equivalent elements occur already for four generators. The paper was received 10 June 1974 and published later that year.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: An established distinction; identities valid in all subspace representations do not automatically hold in the free modular lattice.

title: Subspace systems and direct-sum decomposition
notes: A representation sends meet to intersection and join to sum. A representation of \(D^r\) is exactly a finite-dimensional space \(V\) with subspaces \(E_1^0,\ldots,E_r^0\). Direct sums and indecomposability are defined.
statement: An ordered \(r\)-subspace system is \((V;E_1,\ldots,E_r)\); its morphisms are linear maps carrying every \(E_i\) into the corresponding target subspace. By freeness this is equivalent to a representation of \(D^r\). A direct decomposition is \(V=V_1\oplus V_2\) with \(E_i=(E_i\cap V_1)\oplus(E_i\cap V_2)\) for every \(i\). Finite-dimensional systems decompose into indecomposables, uniquely up to isomorphism and permutation.
reconstruction: The morphisms and simultaneous compatibility condition make the category explicit; arbitrary vector-space complements need not give decompositions of the system.
fate: The subspace-system viewpoint is already present in \citet[\S\S1--2]{gelfandponomarev1971quadruples} and \citet[introduction]{bernsteingelfandponomarev1973coxeter}. Earlier seminar occurrences include 1970-198.1 and 1970-198.13.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established representation theory; the number of subspaces determines the complexity of classification.

title: Classifying all representations of D-r
notes: The explicit problem is ``describe all representations of \(D^r\)''. The ground field is arbitrary and the representations are finite-dimensional.
statement: For fixed \(r\) and field \(k\), classify ordered \(r\)-subspace systems up to a simultaneous linear isomorphism. Over an algebraically closed field, \(r\le3\) has finite indecomposable type; \(r=4\) has a tame classification with one-parameter families. For \(r\ge5\), the problem contains simultaneous similarity of arbitrary pairs \((A,B)\): use \(W\oplus W\) with the two coordinate subspaces, the diagonal, and the graphs of \(A\) and \(B\). An isomorphism preserving the first three is \(g\oplus g\), so the remaining two encode simultaneous conjugacy.
reconstruction: The explicit five-subspace reduction is supplied here. Wildness is a complexity result, not a claim that no mathematically useful invariants or restricted classifications can exist. The four-subspace result quoted is restricted to the field hypotheses of the sources.
fate: The four-subspace classification circulated in the 1970 Tihany contribution and the 1971 announcement \citep{gelfandponomarev1971quadruples}. \citet[pp.~30--32]{bernsteingelfandponomarev1973coxeter} already distinguishes affine families from matrix-pair complexity. Compare earlier occurrences 1972-277.5--1972-277.7. GP-1970-23 concerns a specific deformation example and is not this general problem.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: The finite/tame/wild distinction is established. A request for unrestricted normal forms beyond four subspaces cannot be treated as an isolated unsolved seminar conjecture.

title: Perfect elements and compatible complements
notes: An element is perfect if its image in every finite-dimensional representation over every field admits a complement splitting the representation. Equivalently, its image in each indecomposable is zero or the whole space. Linearly equivalent elements are perfect together.
statement: For a modular lattice \(L\), call \(a\in L\) perfect if each finite-dimensional representation \(\rho\) splits with \(\rho(a)\) as one summand. Equivalently \(\rho(a)\in\{0,V\}\) for every indecomposable \(\rho:L\to\mathcal L(V)\): decompose a finite-dimensional representation into indecomposables and collect those on which \(a\) acts as the whole space. Perfection therefore depends only on the linear-equivalence class.
reconstruction: We explain the equivalence using finite-dimensional decomposition. An arbitrary complement of a subspace is insufficient; it must split every \(\rho(b)\).
fate: This exactly matches the definition in \citet[\S1.2]{gelfandponomarev1974modular}; the proof of the cubicle perfection theorem occupies later sections. Publication followed in 1974.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: An established definition and equivalence. The notebook does not assert that it has classified all perfect elements.

title: Recursive lattice words indexed by adjacent-distinct sequences
notes: The first word is \(e_{i_1i_2}=e_{i_1}\,[\text{overwritten sign}]\,\sum_{k\ne i_1,i_2}e_k\). The next page gives \(e_\alpha=e_{i_1}\sum_{\beta\in\Gamma(\alpha)}e_\beta\), but the conditions defining \(\Gamma\) end in an ellipsis.
statement: The matching published construction is as follows. Let \(\alpha=(i_1,\ldots,i_\ell)\) have adjacent distinct entries in \(\{1,\ldots,r\}\). Let \(\Gamma(\alpha)\) consist of \(\beta=(k_1,\ldots,k_{\ell-1})\) with adjacent distinct entries and \(k_j\notin\{i_j,i_{j+1}\}\) for every \(j\). Put \(e_{(i)}=e_i\) and recursively \(e_\alpha=e_{i_1}\wedge\bigvee_{\beta\in\Gamma(\alpha)}e_\beta\). Empty joins use the least element of the generated bounded lattice.
reconstruction: The meet sign and the completed indexing conditions come from the published formula, not from deciphering the overwritten mark. They are explicitly a literature-based reconstruction. We do not assert that each individual word is perfect.
fate: \citet[\S1.3, equation~(1.1)]{gelfandponomarev1974modular} gives the matching recurrence; the full text was opened and this definition read. The later paper resolves the incomplete source notation without legitimizing silent transcription repair.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: The construction is identified with high confidence; its complete formula is supplied from the 1974 publication.

title: The first Boolean cubicle of perfect elements
notes: The ``trivial perfect elements'' are \(m_t=\sum_{i\ne t}e_i\); the notes say that they generate a Boolean algebra with \(r\) generators.
statement: In the free modular lattice on \(r\ge2\) generators, the sublattice generated by \(m_t=\bigvee_{i\ne t}e_i\) is the first upper cubicle \(B^+(1)\). It is a Boolean lattice with \(2^r\) elements, and every element is perfect. The \(m_t\) are its distinguished coatoms. This is not the free Boolean algebra on \(r\) independent Boolean generators, which would have \(2^{2^r}\) elements.
reconstruction: We identify the cubicle and distinguish lattice generators from freely independent Boolean generators. The minimum and maximum are those of this sublattice, not necessarily those of every ambient representation.
fate: \citet[Lemma~3.1 and Corollaries~4.1--4.2]{gelfandponomarev1974modular} proves the Boolean structure, perfection, and cardinality. These statements give an exact fate for the notebook claim.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established in the 1974 paper. No completeness conjecture for all perfect elements is stated in the notebook and none is added to the problem index.

title: A p-adic homogeneous space as a vertex set
notes: For a \(p\)-adic group \(G\), a maximal compact \(K\) is open, so \(G/K\) is discrete. The example is \(G=\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb Q_p)/C\), with \(K=\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathcal O)\).
statement: For \(G=\operatorname{PGL}_n(\mathbb Q_p)\), let \(K\) be the image of \(\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb Z_p)\). Then \(K\) is compact open and \(G/K\) identifies with homothety classes of full \(\mathbb Z_p\)-lattices in \(\mathbb Q_p^n\). These are vertices of the affine building. For a general reductive group, one quotient by a chosen parahoric need not contain all vertex types.
reconstruction: The quotient image of \(K\), the lattice model, and the restriction to type A are supplied. Maximal compact openness is not asserted for every conceivable topological group.
fate: The affine-building framework is developed in \citet[\S\S2 and 6]{bruhattits1972groupes}, published in 1972. The notebook is an introductory exposition.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established; the quotient and vertex-type qualifications prevent an overgeneralized construction.

title: The standard Iwahori subgroup
notes: The displayed subgroup has integral upper-triangular entries, entries divisible by \(p\) below the diagonal, and unit diagonal entries; it is called Iwahori.
statement: The standard Iwahori subgroup of \(\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb Q_p)\) is \(I=\{g\in\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb Z_p):g\bmod p\text{ is upper triangular}\}\). Its image in \(\operatorname{PGL}_n\) fixes the corresponding alcove in the affine building. A complete lattice chain determines the same stabilizer.
reconstruction: We make the reduction map and passage to the projective group explicit; the notebook's letter \(B\) denotes this compact-open subgroup, not the algebraic Borel of \(G\).
fate: This is standard Iwahori/parahoric structure within \citet[\S\S4 and 6]{bruhattits1972groupes}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established; the matrix display is correct with the group and reduction convention specified.

title: Simplices from common Iwahori stabilizers
notes: Points \(x_i\in G/K\) are identified with conjugates \(K_i\); they span a simplex if a conjugate of the Iwahori subgroup lies in \(\bigcap K_i\).
statement: For \(\operatorname{PGL}_n(\mathbb Q_p)\), distinct lattice-homothety vertices form a simplex when representatives can be ordered in a chain \(pL\subsetneq L_r\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq L_1\subsetneq L\). Equivalently they are a subset of the vertices of one alcove, whose Iwahori fixes them. Vertex stabilizers are the corresponding conjugates of \(K\). Repeated vertices do not enlarge a simplex.
reconstruction: The chain formulation specifies the construction in the example where the notebook's single vertex orbit works. General buildings require all relevant parahoric types.
fate: The simplex/parahoric correspondence belongs to the affine-building construction in \citet[\S\S2 and 6]{bruhattits1972groupes}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established for the stated type-A model; a literal construction from an arbitrary single G/K is too broad.

title: The rank-one Bruhat--Tits tree
notes: For \(n=2\) the complex is declared contractible, with a tree drawn below.
statement: The affine building of \(\operatorname{PGL}_2(\mathbb Q_p)\) is the tree whose vertices are homothety classes of full lattices in \(\mathbb Q_p^2\), with adjacency represented by \(pL\subsetneq L'\subsetneq L\). Its neighbours at \([L]\) correspond to lines in \(L/pL\cong\mathbb F_p^2\), so the valency is \(p+1\). A tree is contractible.
reconstruction: The lattice description and valency explain the drawing. The manuscript does not label it as a finite tree or attach a numerical branching count.
fate: The rank-one instance is contained in the pre-existing affine-building theory of \citet[\S2]{bruhattits1972groupes}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established; the contractibility claim is correct in this example.

title: The finite flag-incidence building in dimension three
notes: In \(V_3(\mathbb F_q)\), vertices of type one are lines and of type two are planes; incidence spans a simplex.
statement: The spherical building of \(\operatorname{PGL}_3(\mathbb F_q)\) has as vertices the nonzero proper subspaces of \(\mathbb F_q^3\); edges are flags \(L\subset P\) with dimensions one and two. It is a bipartite incidence graph, not the contractible affine tree of the preceding item.
reconstruction: We distinguish this finite spherical example from the affine example. No claim that every building in the block is contractible is imputed to the notes.
fate: This is the flag-complex model underlying the building theory used in \citet[\S1, combinatorial background]{bruhattits1972groupes}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established incidence geometry; its type and topology differ from the preceding rank-one affine example.

title: Cancelled rational-function and exponential-sum fragment
notes: Before the curve-counting discussion, crossed-out lines contain \(ax+b/x\) with \(a,b\in\mathbb Z\), a partly illegible superscript, and an exponential-sum fragment.
statement: No summation range, finite field, character, or estimate survives. The fragment cannot identify a definite Kloosterman-sum claim or any other precise exponential-sum theorem.
reconstruction: The visible rational expression is retained as cancelled source evidence. We do not infer the missing summand from a familiar formula.
fate: No exact publication identification is warranted by the cancelled fragment. The subsequent Bombieri discussion is independently identifiable and does not restore this text.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Unidentifiable cancelled material; it has no problem-index entry.

title: The Weil bound and the missing constant one
notes: For a curve \(X/\mathbb F_q\) of genus \(g\), the notes write \(|[X_q]-q|\le2g\sqrt q\) and identify it with the Weil hypothesis.
statement: For a smooth projective geometrically connected curve \(X/\mathbb F_q\) of genus \(g\), \[|\#X(\mathbb F_q)-(q+1)|\le2g\sqrt q.\] Equivalently the reciprocal roots of the numerator of its zeta function have complex absolute value \(\sqrt q\); the equivalence uses the point counts over all finite extensions. An affine curve requires adjustment for omitted points.
reconstruction: Smoothness, projectivity, geometric connectedness, and the extension-field formulation are supplied. For \(\mathbb P^1\), the notebook expression gives \(1\le0\), proving that the missing one matters.
fate: This is the established curve Riemann hypothesis reviewed in \citet[\S I]{bombieri1974counting}. Bombieri's lecture was delivered in June 1973 and printed in 1974; it is not the first proof of Weil's theorem.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established after restoring q+1 and the curve hypotheses; the literal displayed bound is false.

title: A coarse upper bound and the deduction of the full Weil estimate
notes: The notes attribute \([X_q]\le q+4g\sqrt q\) to Stepanov through Bombieri and say that any constant independent of \(q\) would formally suffice for the sharp result.
statement: The Stepanov--Bombieri strategy constructs auxiliary functions to obtain a square-root error estimate and then uses extension fields and suitable covers or twists to recover the zeta-function conclusion. A one-sided upper estimate for one curve over one field, or even only its extension sequence without the necessary companion information, is not the complete deduction. The printed \(q+4g\sqrt q\) also needs an endpoint correction in genus zero.
reconstruction: We retain the method and do not manufacture an exact theorem from the abbreviated constant. Bombieri's hypotheses for the intermediate estimate and the extra covering step are part of the literature, not present in the notebook.
fate: \citet[\S\S~II--III]{bombieri1974counting} is the direct source. Section III explicitly warns that an upper bound alone does not establish the Riemann hypothesis, and supplies the additional argument. The June 1973 circulation predates this talk.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: The method is established; the compressed inference is incomplete and the displayed constant is not quoted as an exact published theorem.

title: Riemann--Roch dimension for a large divisor
notes: For a divisor \(D\), the notes call \(L(D)\) the number of functions divisible by \(D\), and write \(L(D)=\deg D-g+1\) for \(\deg D>2g\).
statement: For a divisor \(D\) on a smooth projective geometrically connected curve, put \(L(D)=H^0(X,\mathcal O_X(D))=\{f\in k(X):\operatorname{div}(f)+D\ge0\}\cup\{0\}\) and \(\ell(D)=\dim_k L(D)\). Riemann--Roch gives \(\ell(D)=\deg D-g+1\) when \(\deg D>2g-2\). The notebook's stronger threshold is sufficient. Over \(\mathbb F_q\), the actual number of elements is \(q^{\ell(D)}\).
reconstruction: We distinguish the vector space, its dimension, and its cardinality, and fix the divisor sign convention.
fate: This is the standard Riemann--Roch input used in \citet[\S~II]{bombieri1974counting}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established; the notebook formula concerns dimension, not the cardinality of a space of functions.

title: Frobenius powers of a Riemann--Roch space
notes: A point \(x_0\) is fixed, \(L_e\) consists of functions with a pole of order at most \(e\) there, and \(L_e^q\) has the same number of elements as \(L_e\).
statement: Assume \(x_0\in X(\mathbb F_q)\) and \(L_e=L(ex_0)\). Then \(f\mapsto f^q\) is an injective \(\mathbb F_q\)-linear map with image \(L_e^q\subset L(qex_0)\), so \(\dim L_e^q=\dim L_e\). It is not the assertion that \(L(qex_0)=L_e^q\). Over an algebraic closure the map is semilinear, with the same dimension conclusion.
reconstruction: The rationality of the base point, the image-space notation, and the increased pole order are supplied.
fate: This Frobenius device is part of \citet[\S~II]{bombieri1974counting}. The notebook retains the essential equal-dimension observation.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established with the image and pole order distinguished.

title: The two multiplication maps in the auxiliary-function construction
notes: A kernel is drawn in \(L_{q-1}\times L_e^q\to L_{q-1}L_e\subset L_{q+e-1}\), with ``isom. tensor prod.'' below. The dimension comparison is \((q-g)(e-g+1)>q+e-g\); the resulting functions vanish on rational points.
statement: Distinguish \(m:L_{q-1}\otimes_{\mathbb F_q}L_e\to L_{q+e-1}\), \(a\otimes b\mapsto ab\), from \(m_q:L_{q-1}\otimes L_e\to L_{q-1+qe}\), \(a\otimes b\mapsto ab^q\). If the recorded dimension inequality applies, \(\ker m\ne0\). For \(v=\sum a_i\otimes b_i\in\ker m\), \(m_q(v)\) vanishes at every rational point except the pole point because \(b_i(P)^q=b_i(P)\). To count zeros one must additionally prove \(m_q(v)\ne0\) and control vanishing multiplicities. The notebook omits these essential steps.
reconstruction: The tensor product and the separation into two maps are our reconstruction from the source method. We do not claim that this bare dimension count by itself proves the square-root bound.
fate: The auxiliary-function and Frobenius-independence argument is in \citet[\S~II]{bombieri1974counting}; the notes compress different spaces and maps into one line. The publication is an exact methodological match, not a validation of the literal diagram.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: The established method works with additional nonvanishing and multiplicity arguments; the notebook diagram has a genuine pole-order mismatch.

title: The announced three-variable case of Serre's problem
notes: Before the speaker heading the notes say: ``\ru{Решена пробл. Серра о мног. от 3-х переменных}''. No coefficient field or characteristic restriction is recorded.
statement: The nearby 1974 result states that every finitely generated projective \(k[x_1,x_2,x_3]\)-module is free when \(k\) is perfect or \(\operatorname{char}k\ne2\). The modern unrestricted theorem holds for every field \(k\) and every finite number of variables. These are different scopes: the notebook alone does not establish the omitted imperfect characteristic-two case in November 1973.
reconstruction: The restriction is supplied from the publication, not read into the handwritten announcement. The all-variable result is its later fate, not a theorem attributed to this meeting.
fate: \citet[Theorem~1 and following remarks]{vasersteinsuslin1974serre}, received 26 November 1973, records work begun in January 1973 and the stated three-variable scope. The unrestricted result followed in 1976: \citet[\S III, Theorem~2]{suslin1976projective} and independently \citet[pp.~167--171]{quillen1976projective}. Their submission dates were 26 February and 1 March 1976 respectively.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Serre's polynomial-ring problem over fields is solved. The 1973 announcement should retain its contemporary scope.

title: Bass stable rank at most two
notes: For every unimodular column \((a,b,c)^t\), there should exist \(\alpha,\beta\in A\) making \((a+\alpha c,b+\alpha c)^t\) unimodular. The scan repeats \(\alpha\) in the second component, despite quantifying \(\beta\). Unimodular is glossed as relatively prime.
statement: For a commutative unital ring \(A\), write \(\operatorname{Um}_r(A)=\{(a_1,\ldots,a_r):\sum Aa_i=A\}\). Then \(\operatorname{sr}(A)\le2\) means that for every \((a,b,c)\in\operatorname{Um}_3(A)\) some \(\alpha,\beta\in A\) give \((a+\alpha c,b+\beta c)\in\operatorname{Um}_2(A)\). Having no common nonunit factor is weaker than generating the unit ideal in a multivariable polynomial ring.
reconstruction: We repair the second coefficient and use the unit-ideal definition. The discussion specializes to commutative rings; noncommutative left/right conventions are not reconstructed unnecessarily.
fate: Bass introduced the stable-range framework \citep[Chapter~I, \S4]{bass1964stable}; \citet[p.~17 and Theorem~1]{vaserstein1971stable} gives the precise unimodular-column formulation before this seminar.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Standard definition, with two independent coefficients and genuine unimodularity.

title: Nonzero K2 forces stable rank three in two variables
notes: The first branch of the displayed theorem is \(\operatorname{sr}k[x_1,x_2]=3\) when \(K_2k\ne0\).
statement: For any field \(k\), if its Milnor group \(K_2^M(k)\) is nonzero, then \(\operatorname{sr}(k[x_1,x_2])=3\). For fields the usual algebraic \(K_2\) agrees with this Milnor group. Bass's dimension bound gives the upper bound three; the nontrivial content is nonreducibility of some unimodular triple.
reconstruction: We specify the field and the \(K_2\) convention. This theorem concerns existence of an obstructed triple, not every triple, and therefore does not contradict the reducibility of the particular conic triple below.
fate: \citet[\S19, p.~994]{vasersteinsuslin1976serre} explicitly attributes this result to \citet{krusemeyer1973fundamental}, published in March 1973 from a submission of June 1972. The precise consequence was read in the former; the original article's chronology was publisher-verified.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established and already available before the talk. The later symplectic formulation is not evidence of a new 1973 theorem by Vasserstein.

title: The unrestricted zero-K2 branch of the stable-rank assertion
notes: The second branch says \(K_2k=0\Longrightarrow\operatorname{sr}k[x_1,x_2]=2\), with no qualification on \(k\).
statement: The verified theorem is \(\operatorname{sr}(k[x_1,x_2])=2\) for fields \(k\) algebraic over a finite field. The notebook's stronger implication for every field with \(K_2(k)=0\) is a definite assertion, but the sources checked here do not establish it. Infinite algebraic extensions of global fields with vanishing \(K_2\) are not excluded by the hypothesis.
reconstruction: We separate the proved algebraic-over-finite-field case from the stronger recorded implication. The absence of a verified modern resolution of the latter in this bounded search is not asserted to mean it is open today.
fate: \citet[Theorem~4 and following remark]{vasersteinsuslin1974serre} prints the same conclusion through the false field implication in item 1973-322.5. The fuller \citet[\S19, p.~994]{vasersteinsuslin1976serre} explicitly leaves the additional field cases unresolved at that time; \citet[introduction]{suslin1980reciprocity} retains the distinction. Class A records publication of the assertion, not proof of its unrestricted validity.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Verified for fields algebraic over finite fields. The unrestricted zero-K2 implication is not settled by the literature verified in this chapter; no present-day C or D claim is made.

title: The erroneous classification of fields with vanishing K2
notes: The parenthesis asserts \(K_2k=0\) for algebraic extensions of finite fields and \(K_2k\ne0\) in every other case.
statement: The forward assertion for fields algebraic over a finite field is correct, but the claimed converse is false: \(K_2(\overline{\mathbb Q})=0\), while \(\overline{\mathbb Q}\) has characteristic zero and is not algebraic over any finite field.
reconstruction: The explicit counterexample answers the literal field assertion. It does not by itself decide the stable rank of \(\overline{\mathbb Q}[x_1,x_2]\).
fate: The erroneous implication is also printed after Theorem~4 in \citet{vasersteinsuslin1974serre}. It is replaced by a more careful statement in \citet[\S19]{vasersteinsuslin1976serre}. The concrete counterexample is recorded in \citet[III, Exercise~6.5, p.~243]{weibel2013kbook}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: False as written; publication of the same claim does not validate it.

title: The real degree obstruction to reducing the sphere row
notes: Under ``example over \(\mathbb R\)'', the column \((x_1,x_2,1-x_1^2-x_2^2)^t\) cannot be reduced; the reason is ``\ru{из степени}''. The coefficients are written \(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb R\), without explicitly saying polynomial functions.
statement: The row \((x,y,1-x^2-y^2)\) is unimodular over \(\mathbb R[x,y]\), because \(x^2+y^2+(1-x^2-y^2)=1\). There are no continuous real-valued \(f_1,f_2\) on the closed unit disk for which \((x+(1-x^2-y^2)f_1,y+(1-x^2-y^2)f_2)\) is everywhere nonzero. Normalization would extend the identity map of the boundary circle to a disk-to-circle map, contradicting its degree. In particular polynomial reduction is impossible over \(\mathbb R\).
reconstruction: The stronger continuous statement and the disk formulation make the recorded degree argument precise. It applies to real-valued functions and cannot be transferred unchanged to complex-valued functions.
fate: This is the obstruction used in \citet[Theorem~8 and its proof, p.~27]{vaserstein1971stable}, received in April 1970 and published in 1971. Our appendix supplies the elementary disk proof for the exact two-variable example.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established. The coefficient field is decisive for the subsequent conic discussion.

title: An incompletely specified algebraic winding symbol
notes: For a curve \(C(x_1,x_2)=0\) and polynomials \(a,b,c\), the notes mention a winding index and a symbol read uncertainly as \(c(a,b)\) or \(e(a,b)\). For \(a=x_1,b=x_2\), it is called the winding number around the origin.
statement: A classical integer winding number requires an oriented real one-cycle avoiding \((a,b)=(0,0)\), together with a map to \(\mathbb R^2\setminus\{0\}\). A symplectic Mennicke symbol instead starts from a unimodular pair in a specified quotient ring and takes values in a specified \(K_1\)-group. The notebook does not say which cycle, field, quotient, or equivalence defines its proposed symbol, so no single exact invariant can be recovered.
reconstruction: The two possible constructions explain the missing data without identifying them. The presence of the next \(K_1\operatorname{Sp}\) definition suggests an algebraic direction but does not prove equivalence with a topological degree.
fate: \citet[\S4, pp.~948--949]{vasersteinsuslin1976serre} defines symplectic Mennicke symbols precisely and is a thematic lead. Searches for the exact conic/index wording did not determine the notebook's symbol or its claimed vanishing criterion.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: The intended invariant is unidentified. The separately displayed function-existence question is concrete enough to analyze without inventing that invariant.

title: Stable symplectic K1
notes: \(K_1\mathrm{Sp}\,B\) is described as symplectic matrices of order \(2n\) modulo elementary matrices.
statement: For a commutative unital ring \(B\), let \(\operatorname{Sp}(B)=\varinjlim_n\operatorname{Sp}_{2n}(B)\) under hyperbolic stabilization and let \(\operatorname{ESp}(B)\) be its elementary symplectic subgroup. Then \(K_1^{\operatorname{Sp}}(B)=\operatorname{Sp}(B)/\operatorname{ESp}(B)\). Stabilization makes the subgroup normal; an arbitrary fixed-rank quotient needs separate stability and normality hypotheses.
reconstruction: The stable direct limit is inserted. The source's unspecified \(2n\) is not treated as an assertion that every finite rank already computes stable symplectic \(K_1\).
fate: The pre-existing symplectic \(K_1\)-functor is recalled in \citet[\S4, Theorem~4.1 and following definition]{vasersteinsuslin1976serre}; the 1974 announcement also explicitly takes the stable union and quotient.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Standard stable definition. It alone does not identify the preceding winding symbol.

title: Reducing the conic triple by entire functions
notes: For \(z_1^2+z_2^2=1\), the notes ask whether the index is zero and, equivalently, whether two functions \(f_1,f_2\), entire or of exponential growth, can make \((z_1^2+z_2^2-1)f_1+z_1\) and \((z_1^2+z_2^2-1)f_2+z_2\) have ``\ru{не имеют общ. делит.}''. They add ``\ru{в полиномах нет, в непр. ф-ях есть}''. The coefficient field is not explicitly restated after the earlier real example.
statement: For the complex formulation put \(c=x^2+y^2-1\). There exist even \(f_1,f_2,A,B\in\mathbb C[x,y]\) with \[A(x+cf_1)+B(y+cf_2)=1.\] In fact take \(f_1=1/2\), \(f_2=(i(x+2)-y)/2\), \(a=x+c/2\), \(s=x+1-iy\), \(A=s(a+1)-a-2\), \(B=is^2/2\). This also answers the complex entire and finite-exponential-type versions. With real-valued continuous coefficients the corresponding nowhere-zero pair is impossible by item 1973-322.6.
reconstruction: We replace the ambiguous ``no common divisor'' by the stronger, stable-rank-relevant unit-ideal condition, and explicitly choose complex coefficients. Literal absence of a common polynomial factor is already satisfied by \(f_1=f_2=0\). The polynomial parenthesis is false for unrestricted complex coefficients, but a lost real-coefficient restriction cannot be ruled out from the notes. The exact relation with the unidentified index is not asserted.
fate: The general entire-function reduction is subsumed by \citet[Theorem~1.1]{brudnyi2019stein}: \(\operatorname{sr}\mathcal O(X)=\lfloor\dim_{\mathbb C}X/2\rfloor+1\), so \(\operatorname{sr}\mathcal O(\mathbb C^2)=2\). The preprint circulated in 2018, publication followed in 2019. It imposes no growth bound. The explicit polynomial certificate is verified here as a critical emendation, without a priority claim or a new C/D designation.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: The stated complex existence problem is settled, including finite exponential type. The historical coefficient restriction and the unidentified index remain source ambiguities, not proved open mathematical problems.

title: Ext from a free resolution
notes: For \(A\)-modules \(M,N\), a free resolution \(\cdots\to M_1\to M_0\to M\to0\) gives \(C^i=\operatorname{Hom}(M_i,N)\), and its cohomology is \(\operatorname{Ext}^i(M,N)\). In degree zero the notes recover \(\operatorname{Hom}(M,N)\).
statement: Let \(A\) be a unital ring and \(M,N\) left \(A\)-modules. Choose a projective resolution \(P_\bullet\to M\), concentrated in nonnegative homological degrees. Set \(C^i=\operatorname{Hom}_A(P_i,N)\) with differential induced by \(P_{i+1}\to P_i\). For \(i\ge0\), \(\operatorname{Ext}_A^i(M,N)=H^i(C^\bullet)\), and \(H^0(C^\bullet)=\operatorname{Hom}_A(M,N)\). Free resolutions exist and suffice.
reconstruction: We specify module handedness, exactness of the augmented resolution, and the grading. Hom and Ext are abelian groups unless extra central coefficient structure is specified.
fate: This is classical homological algebra preceding the seminar. The projective-resolution conventions and existence are checked in \citet[Tag~0643, Definition~13.19.1 and Lemma~13.19.3]{stacks2026foundations}; the total derived interpretation is reviewed in \citet[\S10.7]{weibel1994homological}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established definition, independent of the chosen projective resolution.

title: Comparison of resolutions and the Hom-complex invariant
notes: ``Any two resolutions are homotopic''; the invariant is said to be the complex defined up to homotopy, not merely its cohomology groups.
statement: Two projective resolutions of the same module admit chain maps lifting its identity, unique up to chain homotopy, and these maps are homotopy inverses. Applying \(\operatorname{Hom}_A(-,N)\) gives homotopy-equivalent cochain complexes. Consequently the Hom complex is determined up to chain homotopy by \(M,N\) and the projective-resolution construction.
reconstruction: The phrase ``resolutions are homotopic'' is interpreted as chain-homotopy equivalence of projective resolutions. An arbitrary acyclic augmentation by nonprojective modules does not satisfy the same comparison theorem.
fate: The comparison result is an older part of the theory. A modern precise form is \citet[Tag~0643, Lemmas~13.19.6--13.19.8]{stacks2026foundations}. Its bounded-above projectivity hypothesis also explains the later qualification in item 1973-323.6.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established for projective resolutions; the stronger chain-homotopy invariant is correctly identified.

title: Cohomology groups do not determine chain-homotopy type
notes: The notes warn that complexes can have isomorphic homology groups without being homotopy equivalent, with an analogy to topology.
statement: For complexes of modules, equality of graded cohomology does not determine chain-homotopy type. For example the acyclic complex \(0\to\mathbb Z\xrightarrow{2}\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/2\to0\) is not contractible: a contracting homotopy would split the surjection \(\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/2\), which cannot split. It is quasi-isomorphic to zero but not homotopy equivalent to zero.
reconstruction: The example is supplied as an elementary verification of the recorded distinction; it is not a recovered example of the speaker. This does not conflict with the special comparison theorem for bounded-above projective complexes.
fate: The distinction is built into the older localization construction of the derived category \citep[Chapter~I]{hartshorne1966residues}; \citet[Tag~05RR]{stacks2026foundations} specifies which morphisms are inverted. The particular nonsplit example is checked directly here.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Correct. Merely matching cohomology groups is even weaker than having a specified quasi-isomorphism.

title: The complex of graded homomorphisms
notes: For complexes \(\dot M,\dot N\), the notes write \(\operatorname{Hom}(\dot M,\dot N)\) and describe \(\operatorname{Hom}^i(R,N)\) as maps with shift \(i\), with source and target arrows pointing in opposite directions in the sketch.
statement: For cochain complexes \(P^\bullet,N^\bullet\) of left \(A\)-modules define \[\operatorname{Hom}_A^n(P,N)=\prod_j\operatorname{Hom}_A(P^j,N^{j+n}),\qquad d\phi=d_N\phi-(-1)^n\phi d_P.\] Then \(d^2=0\). Its degree-zero cycles are chain maps, and degree-zero boundaries are null-homotopic maps. For bounded source and target the product is finite in every degree.
reconstruction: The totalization, product convention and differential signs are supplied; the notebook gives only the shifted-map description and a schematic diagram.
fate: The construction is standard and is given exactly in \citet[Tag~0A8H, \S15.73]{stacks2026foundations}. It predates the seminar as part of the homological-algebra framework.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established. The differential is essential: the graded collection of shifted maps alone is not yet the Hom complex.

title: A resolution as a quasi-isomorphism to a complex
notes: A module is regarded as the complex concentrated in one degree. Replacing it by a free complex inducing the same cohomology is called a resolution; the underlined term is quasi-isomorphism.
statement: A chain map \(f:C^\bullet\to D^\bullet\) is a quasi-isomorphism when every \(H^n(f)\) is an isomorphism. A projective resolution of \(M[0]\) is a quasi-isomorphism \(P^\bullet\to M[0]\) with \(P^j=0\) for \(j>0\) and every \(P^j\) projective. More generally a bounded-above complex of modules has a bounded-above projective replacement.
reconstruction: We distinguish a map inducing cohomology isomorphisms from two complexes with merely abstractly isomorphic cohomology. The boundedness is the version justified by the notebook's ordinary resolutions.
fate: See \citet[Tag~0643, Definition~13.19.1 and Lemma~13.19.3]{stacks2026foundations}. These definitions belong to the pre-1973 derived-category theory documented by \citet[Chapter~I]{hartshorne1966residues}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established; arbitrary unbounded replacements require a further resolution theory.

title: When a quasi-isomorphism of free complexes is a homotopy equivalence
notes: The boxed assertion says: two complexes of free modules are quasi-isomorphic if and only if they are homotopy equivalent. No boundedness restriction is repeated.
statement: Every quasi-isomorphism between bounded-above cochain complexes of projective modules is a chain-homotopy equivalence. The unrestricted statement is false. Over \(A=k[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^2)\), the doubly infinite complex with \(P^n=A\) and \(d^n=\varepsilon\) in every degree is acyclic, but not contractible: each possible expression \(dh+hd\) has image in \(\varepsilon A\) and cannot equal the identity. Thus \(P\to0\) is an unbounded counterexample even with rank-one free terms.
reconstruction: The bounded-above convention is a reconstruction supported by the surrounding resolution diagrams. The counterexample checks the need for that convention; it is not attributed to Kazhdan.
fate: \citet[Tag~0643, Lemma~13.19.4 and Remark~13.19.5]{stacks2026foundations} gives the correct bounded-above statement. The notebook's omission does not create a new theorem or question about arbitrary unbounded complexes.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Correct for bounded-above projectives and, more generally, suitable K-projective complexes; false without such a hypothesis.

title: The homotopy category and localization at quasi-isomorphisms
notes: \(K(A)\) has complexes as objects and homotopy classes of maps as morphisms. \(D(A)\) has the same objects; its maps are described as strings of forward maps and backward quasi-isomorphisms.
statement: Let \(K(A)\) be the chain-homotopy category of complexes of left \(A\)-modules. The derived category is the localization \(D(A)=K(A)[S^{-1}]\) at quasi-isomorphisms. Zigzags represent morphisms only after imposing the localization relations; concatenated raw strings are not distinct morphisms merely because their presentations differ. For suitable calculus of fractions one may use roofs \(M\leftarrow P\to N\), with the left arrow a quasi-isomorphism.
reconstruction: The equivalence relation on zigzags and the universal localization property complete the shorthand. Neither a triangulated structure nor later enhancements are claimed to have been fully developed in these two pages.
fate: This is the Grothendieck--Verdier construction already in \citet[Chapter~I, pp.~19--84]{hartshorne1966residues}, based on the Harvard seminar of 1963--1964. The precise localization definition was reread in \citet[Tag~05RR, Definition~13.11.3]{stacks2026foundations}. Related earlier occurrences are 1971-266.3 and 1971-267.1.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established. The quotient relations are part of the definition, and the earlier discussions are expository links rather than recurring open problems.

title: Derived Hom and graded morphisms in the derived category
notes: The stated goal is to make Hom into a complex; the source displays \(\operatorname{Hom}^i_{D(A)}(\dot M,\dot N)\) after constructing Hom from a free replacement.
statement: For \(M\in D^-(A)\), choose a bounded-above projective replacement \(P\to M\). For a complex \(N\), the object \(R\operatorname{Hom}_A(M,N)\) of \(D(\mathbb Z)\) is represented by \(\operatorname{Hom}_A^\bullet(P,N)\). Its cohomology is \[H^iR\operatorname{Hom}_A(M,N)\simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{D(A)}(M,N[i]).\] For modules in degree zero and \(i\ge0\), this is \(\operatorname{Ext}_A^i(M,N)\). For a commutative coefficient ring the usual additional module structure is available.
reconstruction: A derived Hom object is distinguished from the single morphism group in the ordinary category \(D(A)\). The notebook's superscript is interpreted as the graded shifted morphism group, not an intrinsic differential on every ordinary Hom set.
fate: The formulas are checked in \citet[Tags~0A8H and 0A5W, equation~15.75.0.2]{stacks2026foundations}, with projective computation justified by Tag~0643. They are standard derived-category constructions, not a new enrichment theorem of this seminar.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established with the specified replacement and grading conventions.

title: Deriving a contravariant functor by projective replacements
notes: The functor \(F\) is called contravariant, but the diagrams show \(F:M(A)\to M(B)\) and \(\dot F:D(A)\to D(B)\). One chooses free representatives and applies \(F\); cohomology gives ordinary derived functors.
statement: For an additive contravariant left-exact functor \(F:(A\text{-}\mathrm{Mod})^{\mathrm{op}}\to B\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}\), applying \(F\) to a bounded-above projective replacement, with degrees reversed, constructs \(RF:D^-(A)^{\mathrm{op}}\to D^+(B)\). Its cohomology on a module recovers the right derived functors of \(F\). Additivity preserves chain homotopies; bounded-above projective comparison proves independence. A general covariant functor has a different left/right resolution convention.
reconstruction: We restore the opposite category, degree reversal, additivity, left exactness and bounded ranges. Without those data the notebook's covariance diagram and the asserted recovery in degree zero are not a precise theorem.
fate: The bounded derived-functor construction is part of the theory already presented in \citet[Chapter~I]{hartshorne1966residues}. A checked formulation and the role of exactness are in \citet[Theorem~10.5.6 and Remark~10.5.8]{weibel1994homological}, with passage to opposite categories for the contravariant case.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established after repairing variance and specifying the resolution range; arbitrary unbounded free replacement is not sufficient.

title: The universal transformation for a total right derived functor
notes: The last lines require \(QF\to\dot FQ\) and display an isomorphism \[\operatorname{Hom}(QF,GQ)\to\operatorname{Hom}(\dot FQ,GQ)\] for every \(G\), with the arrow pointing right.
statement: Let \(Q_A:\mathcal K_A\to\mathcal D_A\) and \(Q_B:\mathcal K_B\to\mathcal D_B\) be the chosen localizations and let \(F:\mathcal K_A\to\mathcal K_B\) be an additive functor compatible with the relevant triangulated structures. A total right derived functor is \(RF:\mathcal D_A\to\mathcal D_B\) with \(\eta:Q_BF\to RFQ_A\), universal in the sense that composition with \(\eta\) induces the bijection \[\operatorname{Nat}(RF,G)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Nat}(Q_BF,GQ_A),\quad\theta\longmapsto(\theta Q_A)\eta.\] Existence is an additional requirement. For contravariant \(F\), first use the appropriate opposite category.
reconstruction: This states the covariant categorical version consistently. The displayed notebook direction is the inverse factorization map if its universal property has already been established; direct precomposition with \(\eta\) goes the other way. Thus the arrow need not be declared a false theorem, but its intended meaning must be specified.
fate: \citet[Definition~10.5.1, p.~391]{weibel1994homological} states exactly this universal property. The source theory predates 1973; the existence hypotheses are developed in \citet[Chapter~I, \S5]{hartshorne1966residues}. The Stacks formulation also treats existence separately \citep[Tag~05S7]{stacks2026foundations}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: Established universal property. The notebook has a direction ambiguity, not evidence for an additional universal construction beyond standard derived functors.

title: Finite and algebraic general linear groups
notes: The page writes \(G=GL_n(k)\), \(|k|=q\), and \(\underline G=GL(\bar k)\).
statement: For a finite field \(k=\mathbb F_q\) and an integer \(n\ge1\), let \(\mathbf G=GL_{n,\bar k}\). Then \(G=\mathbf G(\bar k)^F=GL_n(k)\), where \(F\) raises entries to the \(q\)-th power.
reconstruction: The subscript \(n\) on the algebraic group and the Frobenius description are explanatory additions.
fate: This is the standard setting of \citet[opening definitions]{green1955characters} (1955), long before the talk. The finite/algebraic distinction is identifiable without reconstructing any missing character formula. The AMS PDF was located but direct opening returned 403, so its entry remains unverified.

title: The first two KdV Lax operators
statement: For smooth real \(u\), as formal differential operators, \([A_0,L]=u_x\) and \([A_1,L]=u_{xxx}-6uu_x\). Thus \(L_t=[A_1,L]\) gives \(u_t=u_{xxx}-6uu_x\); reversing the commutator reverses time.
reconstruction: Operator composition, commutator order, and the resulting sign are made explicit; the sign of the later \(P_1\) on P000541 uses the opposite convention.
fate: \citet[opening equations and \S2]{novikov1974periodic} uses the Lax hierarchy and cites its established antecedents. This is the same general line as 1970-219.1 and 1970-219.6, not a new problem.

title: The real periodic Schrödinger operator is self-adjoint
notes: Gelfand writes \(y^{\prime\prime}+uy=\lambda y\), real periodic \(u\), and says the closure from \(C_c^\infty\) is self-adjoint.
statement: For real smooth \(T\)-periodic \(u\), the operator \(-D^2+u\) on \(C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)\) is essentially self-adjoint in \(L^2(\mathbb R)\); its closure has domain \(H^2(\mathbb R)\).
reconstruction: The uniform convention \(-D^2+u\), \(T>0\), and a sufficient smoothness hypothesis are supplied. Gelfand's displayed \(+D^2\) has the opposite principal sign, so it cannot share all later spectral sign conventions unchanged.
fate: \citet[\S1, pp.~54--58 of the Russian original]{novikov1974periodic} recalls this classical Floquet theory; the paper was received on 18 February 1974 and published later in 1974.

title: Periodic and antiperiodic interlacing
notes: Both boundary conditions carry the same \(\pm\), and the labels occur in pairs: periodic, antiperiodic, antiperiodic, periodic, periodic, and so on.
statement: For real smooth \(T\)-periodic \(u\), impose either \(y(T)=y(0),y_x(T)=y_x(0)\), or both minus signs. The combined eigenvalues satisfy \(E_0<E_1\le E_2<E_3\le E_4<\cdots\); \(E_0\) is periodic and the subsequent boundary types alternate in equal pairs. Equalities mean closed gaps.

title: Self-adjoint Bloch fibers
notes: For every phase \(t\), \(y(x+T)=e^{it}y(x)\) and \(y_x(x+T)=e^{it}y_x(x)\) define a self-adjoint discrete-spectrum problem.
statement: For \(\theta\in\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z\), let \(L_\theta=-D^2+u\) on \(L^2(0,T)\), with domain \(\{f\in H^2(0,T):f(T)=e^{i\theta}f(0),f_x(T)=e^{i\theta}f_x(0)\}\). It is self-adjoint with compact resolvent.
reconstruction: The phase is renamed \(\theta\) to avoid confusion with evolution time.
fate: \citet[\S1, pp.~54--58 of the Russian original]{novikov1974periodic} recalls this classical Floquet theory; the paper was received on 18 February 1974 and published later in 1974.

title: Gelfand transform and its normalization
notes: The lemma writes an integral reconstruction, a quasiperiodicity condition, and an \(L^2\) identity, but mixes period 1 and \(2\pi\), integrates over \(dx\) instead of phase, and drops one subscript.
statement: For \(f\in L^2(\mathbb R)\), define \(Uf(\theta,x)=\sum_{m\in\mathbb Z}e^{-im\theta}f(x+mT)\) first for compactly supported smooth \(f\), then by completion. It satisfies \(Uf(\theta,x+T)=e^{i\theta}Uf(\theta,x)\), \(f(x)=(2\pi)^{-1}\int_0^{2\pi}Uf(\theta,x)\,d\theta\), and \(\|f\|_2^2=(2\pi)^{-1}\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^T|Uf|^2\,dx\,d\theta\). The identities hold in the corresponding \(L^2\) spaces.
reconstruction: The transform itself and a consistent normalization are supplied; the manuscript's three defective displayed identities are retained in the corrections table.
fate: The notes explicitly credit Gelfand's circa-1950 Doklady paper. The concrete normalization here follows Fourier-series Parseval; it is an editorial reconstruction of a classical unitary direct-integral transform. \citet[\S1]{novikov1974periodic} uses the resulting band decomposition.
